sentences.text: The sole known specimen of this extinct waterfowl is a partial skeleton containing an incomplete skull, most of the trunk, a right wing, and fragments of leg bones.
This animal was likely mid-sized for a duck, yet it possessed arm bones, particularly the humerus, that were much stouter than those of any other ducks.
Its ulna was short relative to the humerus and hand, a feature shared with auks and penguins.
The bird had unusually thick arm bones and a short ulna, traits typically found in diving birds like penguins rather than swimming ducks.
Alessandro Portis formally described the species in 1884 under the name Anas lignitifila.
Gerald Mayr and Marco Pavia conducted the first reexamination of the species in a 2014 paper.
The only known specimen of Bambolinetta is a partial skeleton collected in Montebamboli, Tuscany.
A 2014 study reclassified the species as a highly unusual, likely flightless, wing-propelled diver similar to a penguin.
Bambolinetta belongs to the family Anatidae and its parent group is the subfamily Anatinae.
Mayr and Pavia placed the species in its own genus named Bambolinetta based on its type locality.
Fossils of Bambolinetta date to the Late Miocene epoch and are found in Late Miocene deposits in Italy.
The region where Bambolinetta lived formed the Tusco-Sardinian island during the Late Miocene.
The time range for Bambolinetta is the Aquitanian stage, from 23.04 to 20.45 million years ago.
